tagline: The wave travels down the chain
question_text: What happens when you displace the middle mass?
audio_script: I am going to show you how a wave travels through a solid. On screen, three identical masses connected by identical springs. The left spring is attached to a wall. The right spring is also attached to a wall. The two walls are fixed. The masses are free to slide. I displaced the middle mass to the right before pressing play. Watch what happens. The middle mass is pulled back. It swings left. As it swings, the spring on its left stretches. The left mass feels a pull to the right. It starts to move. The spring on the middle mass's right is compressed. The right mass feels a push to the right. It also starts to move. Now watch the three masses at once. The middle mass oscillates between the walls. The left and right masses swing in a slower rhythm, out of phase with the middle. Their motion is driven by the middle mass, not by any direct force. This is a coupled oscillator. Every mass feels a force from its neighbours. The force from each spring is proportional to how far the spring is stretched or compressed. Hooke's law. Newton's second law then gives one equation for each mass. Three equations, coupled together. The solution is a normal mode — a pattern of motion where all three masses oscillate at the same frequency, with different amplitudes. There are three normal modes for this chain. In the lowest mode, all three masses move together, like a single object on one big spring. In the middle mode, the centre mass stays still while the two outer masses swing in opposite directions. In the highest mode, the centre mass moves opposite to both outer masses. The motion we see on screen is a mixture of all three modes. This is what heat actually is. The thermal energy of a solid is stored in the vibrational modes of its atoms. Sound propagates as a wave of coupled oscillators. The same mathematics governs a guitar string, a tuning fork, and the bar of a xylophone.

tagline: The trajectory without drag is not the real one
question_text: How much does air resistance change a projectile?
audio_script: I am going to show you how air resistance changes a trajectory. On screen, two identical objects launched at the same instant, from the same position, at the same speed, at the same angle. They leave the starting point together. The blue trajectory is the idealised case — no air resistance. The yellow trajectory is the real case — with linear drag. Watch what happens. At the start, the two trajectories are almost identical. Over the first tenth of a second you cannot tell them apart. Then the divergence begins. The yellow object peaks slightly earlier than the blue. It reaches a lower peak. By the time it begins to descend, the yellow is already a full body length behind the blue. It lands sooner. It travels less distance. This is drag. Every real projectile experiences it. The drag force on an object depends on its speed — the faster it moves, the more air it has to push aside. The force points opposite to the velocity. For slow objects, the drag is proportional to the speed itself. For fast objects, it grows as the square of the speed. This simulation uses linear drag, so the equations stay solvable. The trajectory is no longer a perfect parabola, but the physics is not mysterious. Drag is just another force. Add it to gravity, and you get the real trajectory. Watch the acceleration arrows on screen. The green arrows show the net force at every instant. In the vacuum case, they point straight down. In the drag case, they tilt backward as the object slows. The engine integrated these equations numerically, step by step, using the Runge-Kutta method. Every arrow on screen was computed from the previous one. This is what a real projectile does. Not a perfect parabola. Not the idealised picture from a textbook. A shape that bends and tapers as the air takes its toll. Every golf ball, every baseball, every cannonball follows this shape. In sport, in ballistics, and in engineering, the ideal parabola is only the first approximation. The real world has drag.

tagline: The period scales as the square root of length
question_text: How does the period change when you double the length?
audio_script: I am going to show you that the period of a pendulum depends only on its length. On screen, two pendulums. The left one has length one metre. The right one has length two point two five metres. I released both at the same angle at the same instant. Watch. The left pendulum swings fast. It completes a full cycle and begins a second. The right pendulum is still in the middle of its first. The left completes three full swings. By that time the right has only completed two. The ratio is one point five. That is exactly the square root of the length ratio. The formula is T equals two pi times the square root of L over g. The left pendulum has period two seconds. The right pendulum has period three seconds. Ratio one point five. This is why the period is independent of the mass. The mass does not appear in the formula. Neither does the amplitude, as long as the swing stays small. Galileo noticed this by watching a chandelier swing in the cathedral at Pisa. He timed the swings against his own pulse. The periods were the same for small and for large swings. He called it isochronism. This is also why the pendulum is the oldest accurate clock. You can regulate a clock by changing the length of the pendulum by a fraction of a millimetre. Nothing else needs to change. Not the mass of the bob. Not the amplitude. Just the length. If you move a pendulum clock from Paris to Quito, the value of g changes slightly, and the clock runs slow. You have to adjust the length to compensate. This is why pendulum clocks have a small screw at the bottom of the bob, so the effective length can be tuned to the thousandth of a millimetre.

tagline: How an integral is actually computed
question_text: What is the area under the curve from zero to two?
audio_script: I am going to show you how an integral is actually computed. On screen, two approximations of the same area. The curve is f of x equals zero point five x squared plus one. We want the area under the curve from x equals zero to x equals two. The top panel uses eight rectangles. The bottom uses thirty-two. Both use the midpoint rule — the height of each rectangle is the value of the function at the middle of that slice. Watch what happens when I switch from the top to the bottom. The eight-rectangle approximation is rough. There are gaps above the curve and overlaps below it. The thirty-two-rectangle approximation fits much more closely. You can see the individual rectangles now, but they hug the curve almost perfectly. The readout on the left shows the actual numerical values. With eight rectangles, the computed area is three point three one. With thirty-two rectangles, three point three two eight. The exact answer is ten thirds, about three point three three three. The approximation gets closer with each refinement. Not because the mathematics is mysterious, but because the slices are smaller and the constant-height assumption is more accurate. In the limit, as the number of rectangles goes to infinity and the width of each rectangle goes to zero, the sum becomes the integral. That limit is the entire content of calculus. Every derivative, every integral, every theorem, comes from this one idea. Slice, approximate, sum, take the limit. And that is what the engine on screen is doing. It is evaluating the function at each midpoint, multiplying by the width, adding the results. That is the midpoint rule. The engine does not know the answer to the integral. It only knows how to evaluate the function. The convergence you see is the convergence of the numerical method.

question_text: What does the magnetic field look like between two parallel wires?
audio_script: I am going to show you a magnetic field you can compute from first principles. On screen, two long straight wires, parallel to each other, both carrying five amperes of current in the same direction. The wires are three metres apart. Watch the field arrows. Around each wire, the magnetic field curls in circles. The field of a single long wire falls off as one over r. Near the wire it is strong. Far away it is weak. But we do not have a single wire. We have two. At every point in space, the field you see is the vector sum of the fields from both wires. Watch what happens between the wires. The field from the top wire points downward. The field from the bottom wire points upward. They oppose. The arrows between the wires are short. Outside the pair — above the top wire and below the bottom wire — the fields point the same way. They add. The arrows there are long. This is superposition. The magnetic field at every point in space is the sum of the fields from every current-carrying element. Because the equations of electromagnetism are linear, contributions from different sources simply add. You can compute the field of a complicated arrangement by adding the fields of its parts. This is what the engine on screen is doing. It samples the field at a grid of points. At each point, it evaluates the field contribution from the top wire, then from the bottom wire, then it adds them. Then it draws the arrows. Every arrow on screen is the actual computed field vector, not a decoration. This same superposition underlies every magnetic device — motors, transformers, inductors, magnetic resonance imaging. When the field of one wire is weak, the field of a nearby wire can dominate. When many wires are packed together, the field pattern becomes complex but is still just the sum of individual contributions. The engine computes it one point at a time.

question_text: What is the pressure drop when water speeds up in a pipe?
audio_script: I am going to show you Bernoulli's equation as a real numerical result. On screen, a pipe with a wide inlet on the left and a narrow throat in the middle. Water flows from left to right. At the inlet, the pipe height is two units. At the throat, it is zero point five. The cross section has narrowed to one quarter of its original area. Watch the fluid particles. They enter slowly. They accelerate through the throat. That is the continuity equation. The same flow rate must pass through the narrow section, so the fluid must speed up by a factor of four. The engine on screen knows the inlet velocity is one point five metres per second. It computes the outlet velocity from A one v one equals A two v two. The throat velocity is six metres per second. Now the pressure. The engine uses Bernoulli's equation. p one plus half rho v one squared equals p two plus half rho v two squared. The inlet pressure was set at two hundred thousand pascals. Plug in the velocities and the density of water. The throat pressure comes out to one hundred eighty three thousand one hundred twenty five pascals. The pressure drops by seventeen thousand pascals. That is a real number, computed from real values. Watch the pressure gauges on screen. The inlet gauge is taller than the throat gauge. The height difference is exactly the ratio of the two pressures. The particles on screen are not animated by hand. Each particle is advanced by the local flow velocity at its position, and the local velocity is computed from continuity. Where the pipe is narrow, the particles move fast. Where it is wide, they move slow. Below the pipe, a hydrostatic tank shows the pressure as a function of depth. Same physics, different geometry. The pressure at the bottom of a three metre tank of water is about thirty thousand pascals above atmospheric. Two different situations, one governing principle.

tagline: How a small extra force changes an ellipse
question_text: What happens to an orbit when a small constant force is added?
audio_script: I am going to show you what happens to an orbit when you add a small extra force. On screen, a planet orbits a star. The gravitational force between them is Newtonian. Inverse square, proportional to the masses. If that were the only force, the planet would trace a perfect ellipse, returning to exactly the same path on every revolution. The orbit would be closed. It would repeat forever. Now watch what happens when I add a small extra force. I have added a constant push on the planet, directed to the right. It is much weaker than gravity. It is a perturbation. Watch the orbit. It is no longer closed. Each revolution, the closest approach to the star shifts. Each time the planet swings around, it ends up on a slightly different path. The shape of the orbit changes slowly. It is still trapped by the star, but the ellipse is not returning to itself. This is called precession. The perturbation is doing a tiny amount of work on the planet, and the energy of the orbit is slowly growing. The semi-major axis grows, the eccentricity changes. The dynamics become more complicated. In real astronomy, orbits precess for several reasons. The gravitational pull of other planets in the solar system. The slight non-sphericity of the central body. Relativistic corrections to Newton's law. Mercury's orbit precesses by forty-three arcseconds per century. That number was one of the first strong tests of general relativity — Newtonian gravity alone could not explain it. In this simulation, the perturbation is much larger than the real relativistic effect. But the physics is the same. Two forces added together, one central and one not. The equations of motion are still Newton's second law. But they no longer have a simple closed-form solution. The engine on screen integrates them numerically, step by step, using the Runge-Kutta method. Every position you see was computed from the previous one. The precision is high enough that you can watch the slow drift of the orbit in real time.

tagline: Two equations two unknowns one answer
question_text: What is the unique solution to this linear system?
audio_script: I am going to show you what a linear system looks like in the language of matrices. On screen, two equations. Two x plus y equals five. x plus three y equals ten. Two variables, x and y. We want the values that satisfy both equations at the same time. The method is called Gaussian elimination. It is the algorithm that runs inside every computer simulation, every optimization problem, every regression. The engine on screen executes it in one step. It builds the augmented matrix. It pivots on the diagonal. It back-substitutes. The solution is x equals one, y equals three. Watch the readout. One and three. Check it. Two times one plus three is five. One plus three times three is ten. Both equations hold. This is the unique solution. Now watch the second panel. It shows the determinant of the coefficient matrix. Two times three minus one times one. That is five. Why does the determinant matter. If it were zero, the matrix would be singular. The system would either have no solution or infinitely many. The determinant tells you whether the solution exists and is unique before you even try to find it. This is why engineers check the determinant of a stiffness matrix before running a finite element analysis. It is why statisticians check the determinant of a covariance matrix before computing a regression. A determinant near zero means the problem is ill-conditioned. Small errors in the input produce large errors in the output. A determinant of exactly zero means the problem is unsolvable — either the equations contradict each other, or they are redundant. The engine tells you which. In this case the determinant is five. The solution is unique, stable, and physical. The same algorithm runs on machines from your laptop to the largest supercomputer. Two equations, two variables, one number that says whether the answer exists. That is linear algebra.

question_text: A spring with damping is released from amplitude A. How does the amplitude decay?
audio_script: I am going to show you how energy leaks out of an oscillator. On screen, a spring with a mass hanging from it. The mass has been pulled down and released. Without any friction, it would oscillate forever at the same amplitude. Now the engine adds damping. Watch the amplitude. Every cycle is a little smaller than the last. Not linearly. Exponentially. If the first swing is one metre, the tenth swing is not nine tenths of a metre. It is much less. The decay follows an exponential curve. A equals A zero times e to the minus gamma t over two. The amplitude drops by a fixed fraction in each fixed interval of time. Watch the energy bar at the bottom. It starts at its maximum. It decays quickly. The energy stored in the spring is proportional to the square of the amplitude. So the energy decays twice as fast as the amplitude. The formula is one half k A squared, and A itself is falling exponentially, so the energy goes as e to the minus gamma t. Now watch what happens as the amplitude becomes small. The oscillation slows down. Not the frequency — the frequency is essentially unchanged. What slows is the visible motion. The mass spends more and more time near the equilibrium point. The peaks and troughs get closer together in height. In a car suspension, the damping is tuned so that after a bump the oscillations die out in about one second. Too little damping and the car bounces up and down for a long time. Too much damping and the ride is harsh. The optimal damping is called critical damping. It is the value that brings the system back to rest as quickly as possible without overshooting. This same physics governs every mechanical system that vibrates. Bridges, buildings, guitar strings, pendulums, atoms in a crystal. Every one of them has a natural frequency and a damping coefficient. Every one of them loses energy to friction and heat.

question_text: What happens to a cube spinning about a vertical axis?
audio_script: I am going to show you a rotating rigid body in three dimensions. On screen, a cube spinning about a vertical axis. This is a three-dimensional scene. The camera moves around the cube so you can see it from several angles. Every point on the cube is moving in a circle. The points near the axis — the top and bottom faces at the center — barely move. The points on the corners, far from the axis, are moving fastest. This is the same physics as a spinning wheel. Every point has the same angular velocity. The linear velocity depends on the distance from the axis. The cube is a special case. Because it is symmetric, its angular momentum vector points along the axis of rotation. If the cube were irregular, the angular momentum would point in a slightly different direction. That direction would precess. This is what happens to a spinning top. It does not just spin. It also wobbles. The mathematics of rigid-body rotation is more complicated than the mathematics of a point mass, because the body has orientation as well as position. To describe it fully, we need not just three numbers — position in x, y, z — but also three orientation angles. The equations of motion become vector equations in three dimensions. The moment of inertia becomes a matrix, not a scalar. Every entry in that matrix depends on the shape of the body and on the axis of rotation. For a cube, the matrix is diagonal, and all three diagonal entries are equal. For an irregular object, the matrix has off-diagonal entries and the dynamics are complex. This is why spacecraft have reaction wheels and why satellites spin about their principal axes. When a body rotates freely without external torque, its angular momentum is constant, but its angular velocity can change. The body can tumble. The mathematics of rotation is the mathematics of three-dimensional orientation. It is the foundation of every flight simulator and every video game engine. Every spacecraft that has ever flown used these equations to plan its orientation.

question_text: How much longer is the period of a pendulum with four times the length?
audio_script: Two pendulums. The left one has length one metre. The right has length two metres. Released at the same instant. Watch. The left one completes three cycles while the right completes about two. The period scales as the square root of the length. Square root of two is about one point four one. So the right pendulum's period is one point four times the left's. But wait — the question asked about four times the length. For that, the ratio would be square root of four, which is two. A pendulum four times as long takes twice as long to swing. This is the useful scaling law.

question_text: A one kilogram ball falls from twenty metres with and without drag. Which lands first?
audio_script: Two identical balls dropped from the same height. The blue one has no air resistance. The yellow one has drag. Watch. At first they fall together. The blue one accelerates freely — its fall is uniform. The yellow one accelerates more slowly. As it speeds up, the drag force grows. At some point the drag equals gravity, and the yellow ball stops accelerating. It reaches terminal velocity and continues falling at a constant speed. The blue ball keeps accelerating. It hits the ground first. This is why raindrops do not kill you — they reach terminal velocity long before they arrive. A raindrop from a cloud two thousand metres up would hit you at over two hundred metres per second if there were no air. With air, it arrives at about nine metres per second.

question_text: At the same temperature which gas molecule moves faster?
audio_script: Two gases in the same box, at the same temperature. On the left, hydrogen. On the right, oxygen. The hydrogen is sixteen times lighter. At the same temperature, the two gases have the same average kinetic energy. But since hydrogen is lighter, its molecules must move faster to carry that energy. The rms speed goes as the square root of the temperature over the molar mass. Plug in the numbers. At three hundred kelvin, hydrogen moves at about nineteen hundred metres per second. Oxygen at the same temperature moves at about four hundred eighty. Ratio four — exactly the square root of sixteen. This is why the Earth's atmosphere has no hydrogen. The hydrogen molecules are fast enough to escape the planet's gravity.
